findings.note: The observability inventory is factually incomplete. The report leaves tokens.merge_id and the relevant stored correlation points unconfirmed and infers absence after grepping only provider_request_id/provider_call_id/token-usage names. Current schema and CRUD already persist tokens.merge_id, provider_id, and ai_run_id; finished ai_invoke_runs persist run_id, token_id, provider_id/provider_name, timing, outcome/exit data, and stdout/stderr tails, and are queryable by group/project. Map these existing managed-run records first, then state the narrower gap accurately: an unmanaged copied-token provider session has no FlowGate run/provider-call/usage telemetry. As written, this misses required scopes 2 and 6 and understates evidence available for incident correlation.

N0002 explicitly requires analysis of client automatic retransmission, but this trigger is not traced. client/shared/api.ts has an Axios response interceptor that replays the original request once after a 401, including POST /api/v1/token/issue and POST /api/v1/ai-invoke/start; postRequest otherwise has no generic transport retry. The report must determine whether authentication rejects the first request before any route side effect (making that replay safe), distinguish timeout/network behavior, and only then exclude this trigger. The current categorical statement that the trigger is always manual is unsupported.

Merely routing copied-token issuance through db_group_ai_leases does not establish the claimed complete prevention. The existing lease lifecycle is managed-run-specific: acquire creates a 120-second acquiring lease, activate requires a run identity and TTL, active ownership is maintained by heartbeat, get_active reclaims expiry, and release is explicit. An unmanaged external session has no worker heartbeat or reliable completion signal. The candidate must identify ownership/lifecycle anchors (activation, lease/token TTL, release on consume/revoke/expiry/merge close/abort, and stale-token rejection). Otherwise admission can reopen while the external session is still working, or the group can remain blocked excessively, so the stated guarantee and risk comparison are incomplete.

ai_review.comment: Revision 2 resolves the prior review findings and the central code-path diagnosis is credible. Three blocking gaps remain in the required observability/trigger analysis and in the guarantee attributed to the shared-admission proposal.

findings.locus: Sections 0 and 7 (classification of the reported phenomenon)
findings.note: The revision correctly concedes that no two-provider-session reproduction or correlated provider telemetry was obtained, but it still says the report is 'at least not merely display/event duplication' and that the losing-worker signal 'exactly' matches B0001. The evidence proves that a real duplicate-invocation-capable path exists; it does not establish which phenomenon actually produced the one-line B0001 observation. Classify the observed incident as undetermined while separately concluding that code permits real duplicate provider sessions.

findings.locus: Section 5, 'same component' trigger bullet and Section 6 reproduction conditions
findings.note: The claim that repeated clicks in one component are safe is false for Copy Mention. Both Vue handlers clear busy immediately after POST /token/issue returns, while token issuance has no group lease or resolver ownership check. A user can therefore click Copy Mention again in the same component, receive T2 after T1, and run both tokens externally. Two concurrently visible panels are not required; distinguish overlapping-request suppression from sequential duplicate issuance and include this simpler trigger.

A short lock around each resolve_conflicts call does not by itself prevent last-write-wins or hybrid results across sequential partial submissions. The report itself establishes that a partial call returns with the session open and leaves its token usable. After call 1 releases the proposed lock, call 2 can acquire it and overwrite the same resolved file, or multiple partial calls can still contribute different files before completion. Such a lock only prevents simultaneous critical-section interleaving; preventing competing resolver writes requires session ownership or a version/CAS/stale-submission rejection. Revise the stated data-integrity guarantee and recommendation.

The statement that the issue is limited to resolve_conflict conflates duplicate invocation with unguarded Git data damage. Section 7 itself acknowledges that copied-token new/edit/chat paths also bypass group_ai_leases, so duplicate external sessions and provider cost can occur there even if document revision CAS rejects or contains the eventual write. Limit only the silent Git overwrite consequence to resolve_conflict, and describe the admission/cost exposure separately.

findings.locus: Sections 9-11, merge:{merge_id} lock anchor and unresolved item
findings.note: The report leaves acquisition of the merge:{merge_id} lock untraced and uses that uncertainty as a deadlock risk for candidate 1, although repository-wide searches resolve it: merge: literals occur in release calls, legacy-cleanup comments/docstrings, and recovery handling, while no acquisition assigns that holder; finalize explicitly says not to transfer the lock. State that the current code does not acquire this session holder and treat the releases as legacy leftovers, then assess any new lock design from that actual baseline. This is required by the requested lock scope/lifetime analysis.

The citation 'ACQUIRING_TTL_SEC=25' reads as a 25-second constant and contradicts Section 3-2. Source line 25 defines ACQUIRING_TTL_SEC = 120. Rewrite it as 'ACQUIRING_TTL_SEC = 120 (group_ai_leases.py:25)' so the timing analysis is unambiguous.

ai_review_history.comment: The revised report materially improves the prior version and its central code-path finding is credible: copied resolve_conflict tokens bypass the managed-run lease and competing submissions can reach an unlocked write path. It still needs corrections to incident classification, trigger coverage, impact scoping, and especially the guarantee attributed to a request-scoped Git lock before it meets the investigation requirements.

findings.note: The evidence proves that two independently issued resolve_conflict tokens can target the same open merge session, but it does not prove that two external provider requests actually occurred. Step 2 explicitly says an external AI need not be invoked, and step 4 calls the resolve endpoint directly; that reproduces concurrent Git submissions, not duplicate external AI calls. This does not satisfy N0002 scope 6 or its requested mapping of run/request/provider IDs, token usage, and stored events/logs. Recast the conclusion as a code-proven possibility unless a two-provider-session reproduction or correlated telemetry is supplied.

The claimed one-consumption guarantee is inaccurate for resolve_conflict requests. post_merge_resolve_token consumes the token only after resolve_conflicts returns merged or resolved_pending_review (git_routes.py:516-519); partial successful calls that remain in conflict leave the token usable. Therefore one token can submit multiple partial requests, and token consumption is not a per-request deduplication boundary as the table states.

The bullet labels cross-panel operation as the real vulnerability and includes clicking AI invoke in both panels, but Section 4 correctly establishes that concurrent AI-invoke starts for the same group are atomically rejected by group_ai_leases. Only the AI-invoke plus unmanaged copied-mention combination bypasses the shared admission guard. The stated trigger set should exclude the two-AI-invoke case or explicitly say its second start is rejected.

Serializing git_service.resolve_conflicts is described as the fundamental solution and top candidate, but it cannot prevent either external AI session from starting and cannot prevent the doubled provider cost identified in Section 7. It only protects the Git write/commit critical section. The report must distinguish data-integrity containment from duplicate-invocation prevention; preventing the reported invocation duplication requires shared admission or resolver ownership across both token issuance and ai-invoke start before provider launch.

ai_review_history.comment: The report has a strong code-path inventory and correctly identifies the admission gap between managed AI invoke and copied-token execution. However, it overstates the evidence as an actually demonstrated external-call duplicate, misstates token consumption semantics, and recommends a consumer-side lock as though it prevented the duplicate invocation itself. These points affect the central verdict and required remediation comparison.
